subChunks.title: Classes, Objects & Encapsulation
subChunks.hookHtml: Every wizard is unique — a name, a rank, a mana reserve, a set of spells. Object-Oriented Programming lets you create a blueprint for a wizard and then stamp out as many wizards as you need.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Classes and Objects

A class is a blueprint. An object is a specific instance created from that blueprint.

public class Wizard {
    // Fields — the object's state
    private String name;
    private int mana;

    // Constructor — called when creating an object
    public Wizard(String name, int mana) {
        this.name = name;  // 'this' refers to the current object
        this.mana = mana;
    }

    // Method — the object's behaviour
    public void castSpell() {
        if (mana >= 10) {
            mana -= 10;
            System.out.println(name + " casts a spell!");
        } else {
            System.out.println(name + " is out of mana.");
        }
    }

    // Getters — controlled read access
    public String getName() { return name; }
    public int getMana()    { return mana; }
}

Creating objects:

Wizard w1 = new Wizard("Lyria", 100);
Wizard w2 = new Wizard("Drake", 50);
w1.castSpell(); // Lyria casts a spell!
w2.castSpell(); // Drake casts a spell!

Encapsulation

Encapsulation means keeping fields private and exposing controlled access through public methods. This prevents outside code from putting a Wizard's mana into an invalid state (like -999).

The this keyword

this.name = name disambiguates between the field (this.name) and the constructor parameter (name).

toString()

Override toString() to give your objects a readable description:

@Override
public String toString() {
    return name + " (mana: " + mana + ")";
}

storyBeats.text: Eldrin escorts you to a vast workshop filled with hundreds of identical bronze wizard figurines — each one unique only in the inscription on its base.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Observe. One mould. Hundreds of wizards — each with its own name and mana. That mould is a class. Each figurine is an object. This is the heart of Object-Oriented Programming.

storyBeats.speaker: The Wizard blueprint
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Notice the word private before the fields. That is encapsulation — the mana is locked inside the Wizard. No outside code can scribble in an invalid value. Access is through getter methods only.

storyBeats.speaker: Creating and using objects
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: And one more craft: override toString() so that when you print a Wizard object, you get useful information instead of a memory address. The @Override annotation tells the compiler you are intentionally replacing a method from the parent class.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Create a Spell class with:

  • Two private fields: String name and int manaCost
  • A constructor that sets both fields
  • A method cast(int currentMana) that returns a String: "[name] cast! (cost: [manaCost])" if currentMana >= manaCost, otherwise "Not enough mana to cast [name]"
  • A toString() that returns "Spell: [name] ([manaCost] mana)"

In the public class Main entry point, create two spells: Fireball (cost 30) and Heal (cost 10). Print each, then call cast(25) on each and print the result.

questions.questionHtml: What keyword creates a new object in Java?
questions.explanationHtml: The new keyword allocates memory on the heap and calls the constructor: Wizard w = new Wizard("Lyria", 100);.

questions.questionHtml: Encapsulation means making all fields public so other classes can access them freely.
questions.explanationHtml: Encapsulation means making fields private and providing controlled access through public getter and setter methods. This protects the object's internal state from invalid modifications.

questions.questionHtml: What is the primary purpose of the this keyword in a constructor?
options: It calls the parent class constructor
It disambiguates between a field and a parameter with the same name
It creates a new copy of the object
It prevents the object from being garbage-collected
questions.correctAnswer: It disambiguates between a field and a parameter with the same name
questions.explanationHtml: this.name refers to the instance field; name alone in a constructor parameter shadows the field. this.name = name correctly assigns the parameter to the field. Without this, you'd be assigning the parameter to itself.

subChunks.title: Inheritance, Interfaces & Polymorphism
subChunks.hookHtml: A FireWizard is a Wizard. A HealerWizard is a Wizard. Both share a common core but have distinct abilities. Java's inheritance and interfaces let you model this naturally.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Inheritance — extends

public class Wizard {
    protected String name;
    protected int mana;

    public Wizard(String name, int mana) {
        this.name = name;
        this.mana = mana;
    }

    public void castSpell() {
        System.out.println(name + " casts a basic spell.");
    }
}

public class FireWizard extends Wizard {
    private int firePower;

    public FireWizard(String name, int mana, int firePower) {
        super(name, mana);  // calls parent constructor
        this.firePower = firePower;
    }

    @Override
    public void castSpell() {
        System.out.println(name + " casts Fireball — power: " + firePower);
    }
}

Polymorphism

A parent-type variable can hold any subclass object. Method calls resolve to the actual object's implementation at runtime (dynamic dispatch):

Wizard w = new FireWizard("Ignis", 100, 80);
w.castSpell(); // prints FireWizard's version!

Interfaces — contracts without implementation

public interface Healable {
    int heal();      // abstract by default
    default void reportHeal() {
        System.out.println("Healed " + heal() + " HP");
    }
}

public class Cleric extends Wizard implements Healable {
    @Override
    public int heal() { return 50; }
}

Interfaces define a contract. Any class that implements the interface promises to provide those methods. Unlike abstract classes, a class can implement multiple interfaces.

abstract classes

public abstract class MagicUser {
    public abstract void castSpell(); // subclass must implement
    public void rest() { System.out.println("Resting..."); }
}

storyBeats.text: The Academy courtyard is full of specialised wizards — fire-wielders, healers, illusionists. Eldrin gestures at the crowd.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: They are all wizards. They all have names and mana. Yet each has a special ability. Rather than writing a completely new class for each type, we build on a base class. The child class inherits everything from the parent and adds its own twist.

storyBeats.speaker: FireWizard extends Wizard
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: This leads to polymorphism — many forms. A single Wizard reference can point to any subclass. When you call castSpell() on it, Java calls the subclass version at runtime. This is dynamic dispatch, and it is extraordinarily powerful for writing flexible code.

storyBeats.speaker: Polymorphism
storyBeats.text:
Wizard w = new FireWizard("Ignis", 100, 80);
w.castSpell(); // calls FireWizard's version

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Interfaces are contracts. They say: any class that implements me must provide these methods. Unlike classes, a single class can implement multiple interfaces — a wizard can be both Healable and Combatant simultaneously.

questions.questionHtml: What keyword does a subclass use to call its parent's constructor?
questions.explanationHtml: super() calls the parent class constructor and must be the first statement in the subclass constructor. this() calls another constructor in the same class.

questions.questionHtml: How many interfaces can a Java class implement?
questions.explanationHtml: A Java class can implement any number of interfaces (separated by commas). This is one advantage over abstract classes, of which a class can extend only one.
Even though the variable type is A, the actual object is a B. Java uses the overriding method in the actual object's class — this is polymorphism / dynamic dispatch.

questions.questionHtml: When should you use an interface rather than an abstract class?
options: When you want to share implementation logic between related classes
When you need multiple inheritance — a class must fulfil several unrelated contracts
When all methods should be final
When you need constructor code to run at instantiation
questions.correctAnswer: When you need multiple inheritance — a class must fulfil several unrelated contracts
questions.explanationHtml: Use an interface when you want to define a contract that unrelated classes can fulfil (e.g., Comparable, Runnable). Use an abstract class when you want to share code among closely related classes in a hierarchy. A class can extend only one abstract class but implement many interfaces.
